cells.tense: Right now you're here with it, asking real questions about what you want.
cells.ask: Tell one person a decision you're about to make, out loud, and where it stands now — before you've got it sorted. Watch how much easier the next step gets once someone else has heard which way you're leaning.
cells.core:
You're asking real questions about what you want, and you can sit in a question for a while. You turn things over, you listen, you let what you find change your mind. People get more honest around you, because you don't perform knowing something you don't.

The questioning has been good for what pulls you, but it's been mostly a private thing. What it's ready to feed next is a choice you make and stand behind — and that's lopsided with how much you investigate. Saying one intention out loud, while it's still unformed, sounds careless when your whole method is to study things first. So say it anyway, to a person who'll just hold it. You don't lose the inquiry — you find out what it was walking toward.
cells.sheetLine: You ask real questions about what you want, and you don't flinch at the answers.
cells.verb: asking your way into what's true
cells.place: the part of you turned toward what it wants

cells.tense: You're already living in how it all works out, and bracing for the moment it doesn't.
cells.ask: Ask one real question and leave it unanswered for a few hours. Notice what you want to do with the gap before you do it.
cells.core:
You're ahead of the present, pre-living how it all plays out, rehearsing what you'll say and what they'll say back. Gathering and questioning stopped being how you find out — now they're how you keep from being caught not knowing. Things don't get to arrive as themselves, because you've already decided what they mean before they do.

A question left open sounds like sitting in the dark when your whole body wants to be holding the answer. Here's what it can look like when it's working well: people who study a thing closely end up comfortable not knowing yet, and what they perceive lands without argument because they've sat with the question long enough. Pick one thing you're dying to know the outcome of and don't chase it. Just watch what happens in you while it's unresolved. The gap may hold more than the answer was going to.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped asking so you can stop being unsure.

cells.tense: You stopped showing up to your own questioning a while back and you're still watching the door.
cells.ask: Pick something you have a hunch about and follow a simple next step on it today — text one person, look up one thing, take one step you decided on. Let the hunch carry you instead of waiting for a reason.
cells.core:
Somewhere along the way you stopped asking your own questions — not because the ability isn't there, but because what came back made asking feel like a bad idea. So you stay where things can't reach you, and the pull that used to point you at something now just points at the fact of pulling. Trying harder to get curious won't work; you can't push a thing forward that isn't there to push.

But something else is still live in you: the part that can wonder, that follows a half-formed idea out of sheer interest, that fills in the shape of what might be before it's real. That part is intact. Meet it halfway — a hunch, a small curiosity, a step toward something that catches your attention — and the movement is what carries you back toward wanting. Not the other way around.
cells.sheetLine: You quit asking before you ever got your answer, and you're still watching the door.
cells.verb: asking your way into what's true
cells.place: the part of you turned toward what it wants

cells.tense: You're keeping what you want at arm's length, and calling that just being reasonable about it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you want that you've been calling a smart delay, and say it out loud plainly — no qualifiers, no reasons, no timeline. See what it sounds like without the machinery around it.
cells.core:
You've been steering by what you want for a while now, in detail — which is worth noticing, because if someone asked you how you're doing on it, you'd probably say you're still figuring it out. But the plan is already there. You decide around what pulls you. What's unspoken isn't the want; it's that the want is already taking the shape of a plan.

Somewhere in there the whole thing got handed to a story about timing or readiness. The version underneath is plainer than that: something is worth caring about, and you'd be able to say what it is without translating it into something that sounds less interesting. Say one of them plainly and see how much smaller the translation was than the thing.
cells.sheetLine: You're not still deciding. You're translating.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is any hint of what happened before the offering stopped or why absorbing took over the wanting — the record gives only the capacity, the seat and the status, so the cells stay on the mechanism and leave the story to the live Reader. The reader could fairly say the mechanism isn't the fault — pushing everyone to care could come from generosity, not from closing a gap — so each cell names the bend as the capacity in excess, not as a motive, and the ask survives being wrong because it's one act at the table that teaches something either way. The sentence serving the writer most is the closing aphorism about tracing the wanting, so it gets cut and the close gets plain words instead.
